items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Yusef was one of the profound saxophone players in the 40s that changed

ctx.x: What was his frame of mind for you?

It was civil unrest. Well he was very spiritual but the thing is a musician plays the life of the environment. He was affected from the environment. You know I’m talking about people like Martin Luther King and all the struggles that went in terms of civil rights or voting rights or women. We struggle with that today. You know? Same thing. It never ends. And then everybody was very spiritual too at that particular time. Because to play the music I think you had to have a spiritual awareness about you. These guys…

I’d like to get at an issue and start with a quote. The issue is the role of jazz in society and how society affects jazz. And this is a quote from Max Roach that was connected to the “We Insist Freedom Now” LP, it was 1962. And he said “We American jazz musicians of African descent have proved beyond all doubt that we’re master musicians of our instruments. Now what we have to do is employ our skill to tell the dramatic story of our people and what we’ve been through.” So my question to you is did that music…
